header.title: Traditional AGV Dispatching in an Automated Container Terminal under Stochastic Conditions

rows: Briskorn inventory rule, nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS), fixed groups
Memetic search on the expected times, plan made once then followed
Re-plans every 10 crane handovers, keeping the decisions taken, with and without thinking time
Preference learning or imitation of the benchmark
Best known plan, as it knows all future times

findings.text: The simulator reproduces an independent answer key to within a millionth of a second, its rack rules give the expected outcome in every check, and AGVs never collide or deadlock in traffic.
findings.conditions: 5 answer-key cases · 216 random runs · 780 automatic tests

findings.text: Six AGVs per crane is the operating fleet. The best rule then keeps each crane waiting 3.4 s per container, against 7.8 s for random dispatching, so the choice of dispatcher clearly matters.
With twelve AGVs every rule needs to see ten jobs ahead of each crane. With that, NV/FCFS reaches 3.4 s per container, and seeing further adds nothing.
findings.conditions: No randomness · 12 AGVs · windows of 1 to 50 jobs · 30 test instances

findings.text: The size of the ship does not change the comparison. What lowers the waiting is fewer switches between discharge and loading, not fewer containers.
findings.conditions: No randomness and ±20% · 10, 12 and 14 AGVs · 24 to 400 jobs per crane · 30 instances

findings.text: At the operating fleet of 12 AGVs the search finds 90 to 100% of the room for improvement on ships where the exact best is known. It serves as the perfect-information benchmark, read as the best plan known.
findings.conditions: Every order list tried · 12 and 16 jobs · 6 and 12 AGVs · ±0% and ±30%

findings.text: Even with crane times varying by ±40%, a dispatcher that knew the future would remove 57% of the best rule's waiting, while a plan made in advance loses its whole 2.3 s lead over NV/FCFS. A real-time dispatcher has room to win.
findings.conditions: ±0 to ±40% crane times · 12 AGVs · standard ship · 30 instances

findings.text: Re-planning makes the GA the strongest traditional method at every level of randomness. But its lead over the best rule shrinks from 1.0 s at ±10% to 0.2 s at ±40%, and it stays 1.6 s above the benchmark, because it cannot see future crane times.
findings.conditions: Re-plan every 10 handovers · ±0 to ±40% crane times · 12 AGVs · 30 instances

findings.text: Waiting 54 s for each new plan costs the re-planning GA 0.43 s per container at ±40%, and a 1.6 s search finds worse plans. Either way it is no better than the best rule on each instance, and stays over 2 s above the benchmark. No traditional method closes the gap in real time.
findings.conditions: Thinking time 1.6 to 183.6 s · ±0 to ±40% crane times · 12 AGVs · 30 instances

findings.text: Random AGV speeds wear down a plan made in advance as well. Its lead over NV/FCFS falls from 2.26 s with exact speeds to 0.62 ± 0.65 s with speeds varying by ±20% per trip, ahead on only 18 of 30 instances.
findings.conditions: ±0 to ±20% AGV speed per trip · crane times as planned · 12 AGVs · 30 instances

findings.text: With both kinds of randomness, the plan made in advance is no longer clearly ahead of NV/FCFS, −0.39 ± 0.57 s. Re-planning keeps a clear lead of 1.15 ± 0.64 s per container, winning 25 of 30 instances, but stays 1.57 s above the benchmark.
findings.conditions: Crane times ±20% and AGV speeds ±10% together · 12 AGVs · 30 instances

stages.question: Can the simulator be trusted?
stages.why: Every later number depends on the simulator moving AGVs exactly as the layout and vehicle data say.

stages.question: Where do dispatching decisions matter?
stages.why: Before adding randomness, the fleet size and rule settings must be chosen where the choice of dispatcher can make a difference.

stages.question: Is the optimiser strong enough to serve as a benchmark?
stages.why: The benchmark and the optimised plans both come from a search, so the search itself has to be checked first.

stages.question: What happens when crane times and AGV speeds become random?
stages.why: This is the core test of the traditional baselines, and the reason a real-time dispatcher is needed.

notation: How much crane cycle times vary. Each cycle is drawn as $c_i \sim U\big((1-\delta)\,\bar c,\ (1+\delta)\,\bar c\big)$ with $\bar c = 75$ s, so with $\delta = 0.4$ each cycle takes between 45 and 105 s instead of exactly 75 s.

The number after ± is half the width of a 95% confidence interval over the $n$ seeds, $\bar I \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt{n}$, where $s$ is the standard deviation over the seeds and $t = 2.045$ for 30 seeds.

Each seed fixes one instance and one draw of crane times, and every method runs on the same seeds. The gap between two methods A and B is therefore measured seed by seed, $\Delta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(I_{A,k}-I_{B,k})$, under identical conditions (common random numbers).
Nearest vehicle, first come first served. A free AGV takes the oldest released job.
The benchmark sees all realised crane times in advance. No real dispatcher can, so it shows how much room is left.

cards.title: The simulator matches an independent answer key, and AGVs never collide
cards.lead: Yes. In 5 answer-key cases with 190 event times and 308 path segments, the largest gap is 5 × 10⁻⁷ s, below the required millionth of a second. The rack rules and the traffic cases give the expected outcome in every check. In 96 random runs on the full yard and 120 stress runs, no two AGVs ever collided, came inside each other's braking distance, used one rack at the same time, or locked each other in.
cards.body: The answer-key cases were built on the earlier 5-block section of the yard, at one speed and with 9 m turns, where every path can be traced step by step. They check the core motion and crane rules. The newer physics of the current model (slower loaded AGVs, 10 m turns, traffic, speed variation) is checked separately: by the rack and traffic cases, the collision checker and the stress runs. The checker is not blind, since on the earlier model without traffic it finds overlapping bodies at 1,362 sampled moments of a single run. A suite of 780 automatic tests repeats all of these checks after every change to the code.
details: Single trips, rack visits, lane booking at the buffer, a crane with all four lanes full, a single open lane, parking, and loads fetched from racks.
AGVs drive at 6 m/s on straights and 3 m/s in turns of 10 m radius, with 0.5 m/s² acceleration and braking (Luo, 2016). A loaded AGV is limited to 3.5 m/s (Zhao et al., 2025).
Each trip reserves the space its body and braking distance will cover, and starts later if that space is taken. AGVs wait only where they stand, never on the road.
Driving 15.5 m into the rack lane and back at 1 m/s, as in the earlier 46 s visit. Raising and lowering the platform take 10 s each, an assumption since no published value was found.
Every event time must agree within 10⁻⁶ s, every segment length within 10⁻⁶ m.
cards.label: Experiment 1.1 · Simulator check

design.question: Does the simulator move AGVs, cranes and racks exactly as the layout, the vehicle data and the rules say, and does it keep AGVs apart in traffic?
design.why: Every later number comes from the simulator. If it moved AGVs wrongly, every comparison of dispatchers would be wrong with it. It matters even more for the learning dispatchers (DQN, PPO, MAPPO), which are trained inside this simulator. A rule or a plan can only be misled by a simulator error, but a learning agent tries many actions and keeps whatever earns reward, so it will find an error and use it. In the earlier model without traffic, AGVs passed through each other in every run. An agent trained there could learn to send many AGVs down one lane at no cost, a policy that looks excellent in training and fails on a real terminal. The physics (speeds, turns, rack steps, traffic, safe distances) sets what an agent is allowed to learn, and the same rules apply to every method, which keeps the comparison fair.
design.vary: Small cases that each exercise one rule. Single trips, lane booking under the crane, waiting at a full crane, parking, choosing the nearest free rack, a block whose racks are all busy, the steps of a rack visit, an AGV catching up with a slower loaded one, and two AGVs at one crossing. Then many random runs with traffic.
design.fixed: Every expected value comes from outside the simulator. The answer key is a separate script that imports none of its code. The rack and traffic cases have outcomes that follow directly from the rules. The collision checker reads only the positions the simulator records, not its traffic control.
design.measure: The largest gap between the simulator and the answer key, over every event time and every path segment, and the number of collisions and deadlocks in random runs.
design.decide: The simulator passes only if every gap is below a millionth of a second, every rack and traffic case gives the expected outcome, and no random run has a collision or a deadlock.

maths.step: Speed where two path segments meet
maths.text: A path is a chain of straights (at most $v = 6$ m/s) and turns (at most 3 m/s, *Luo, 2016*). The AGV starts and stops at rest and accelerates and brakes at $a = 0.5$ m/s². Going forward, the speed $w_{i+1}$ at the end of segment $i$ of length $L_i$ is what the AGV can reach from $w_i$. A backward pass then lowers it wherever the AGV could not brake in time.

maths.step: Time to drive one segment
maths.text: Inside a segment the AGV speeds up, cruises and slows down. If the peak speed $v_p$ stays below the limit $V$ there is no cruise. For a 100 m straight from rest to rest, $v_p = \sqrt{50} = 7.07$ m/s is above 6 m/s, so the AGV cruises.
maths.tex: $$v_p = \sqrt{a L + \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0^{2}+v_1^{2})},\qquad t = \begin{cases}\dfrac{2v_p - v_0 - v_1}{a} & v_p \le V\\[8pt] \dfrac{2V - v_0 - v_1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{V}\Big(L - \dfrac{V^{2}-v_0^{2}}{2a} - \dfrac{V^{2}-v_1^{2}}{2a}\Big) & v_p > V\end{cases}$$

maths.step: Length of a rack visit
maths.text: The AGV drives $\ell = 15.5$ m into the rack lane and back at $v_r = 1$ m/s, and raises and lowers its platform in 10 s each. A discharge places the container after raise, drive in and lower. A load lifts it after drive in and raise.

maths.step: Safe distance behind another AGV
maths.text: With traffic, an AGV may only be where it could still stop before reaching the AGV ahead. Its body length $L = 14.8$ m plus its braking distance at speed $v$, with braking rate $a = 0.5$ m/s², must stay clear of the other body.

maths.step: The pass criterion
maths.text: Every event time of the simulator is compared with the value in the independent answer key, and the largest gap must be below a millionth of a second.

cards.title: Six AGVs per crane keep the cranes busy, more start to crowd the roads
cards.lead: The cranes wait less with every AGV added, down to 2.9 s per container at 13 AGVs. With more AGVs the roads get crowded and the waiting rises again. With 12 AGVs, six per crane, the best rule (NV/FCFS) keeps each crane waiting 3.4 s per container while random dispatching wastes 7.8 s, so the later experiments use 12 AGVs.
cards.body: The yard is long and a loaded AGV drives at only 3.5 m/s, so each container needs 264 s of AGV work, about 3.5 crane cycles. Two cranes therefore need at least 7.0 AGVs even with perfect sharing. With two AGVs per crane the cranes manage 25.2 moves per hour, about 17% below the 30.5 reported by Luo (2016), whose simulation uses its own tool and assumptions. From 14 AGVs on, AGVs start to block each other on the roads. The Briskorn rule suffers most, 6.6 s at 14 AGVs and 20.4 s at 16, while NV/FCFS stays between 3.1 and 5.0 s.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. AGVs drive at up to 6 m/s when empty and 3.5 m/s when carrying a container (Zhao et al., 2025), turn on a 10 m radius (Luo, 2016b) and share the roads: each AGV books the road ahead of it, its body plus its braking distance, so AGVs wait for each other and never collide (model v5). No randomness.

It is close to the lowest waiting, splits evenly over the two cranes, and random dispatching still wastes about twice as much as the best rule. Luo (2016) reports that terminals usually run 5 to 8 AGVs per crane. Fleets of 10 and 14 are kept as a scarce and a crowded case.
The Briskorn inventory rule with phase factor 1.6 (Briskorn et al., 2006), nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS) with a window of 10 jobs, fixed crane groups, and random dispatching.
30 seeds, with every method run on the same seeds. Means are shown with a 95% confidence interval (t = 2.045).
cards.label: Experiment 2.1 · Fleet size

design.question: How many AGVs do the two cranes need on this yard, and at what fleet size does the choice of dispatcher make a difference?
design.why: Every later experiment runs with one fleet. With too many AGVs, spare vehicles hide every dispatching mistake and all methods look the same. With too few, no method can keep the cranes busy. The comparison is only meaningful in between.
design.vary: The fleet, from 2 to 16 AGVs (1 to 8 per crane), and the dispatching rule, all four rules.
design.fixed: No randomness, so every crane move takes exactly 75 s. Each run has 200 containers on the 50-block yard. Each fleet and rule is run on the same 30 instances.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container, the mean over the 30 instances with its 95% confidence interval.
design.decide: The smallest even fleet at which the good rules leave little waiting while random dispatching still wastes clearly more. Checked against the crane productivity reported by Luo (2016).

maths.step: The work an AGV does for one container
maths.text: Each container needs a trip between crane and yard, the drive to the next job, and one rack visit of $r = 51$ s. Here $d$ is the driving time per container, all AGV legs added up and divided by the $n$ containers, averaged over the 30 instances and all fleet sizes.

maths.step: The fewest AGVs that could keep both cranes busy
maths.text: Each crane needs one AGV every $c = 75$ s, and one AGV can serve a container only every $\bar W$ s. So $m = 2$ cranes need at least the number below. It is a lower bound, since it assumes AGVs never wait and are shared perfectly, which is why the cranes still wait with 10 AGVs.

maths.step: From waiting time to crane productivity
maths.text: A crane completes one move every $c$ seconds plus the time $\bar I$ it waits for AGVs, so its moves per hour are given below. With two AGVs per crane this is about 17% below the 30.5 moves per hour reported by *Luo (2016)*, because loaded AGVs drive at only 3.5 m/s here. Luo used a different simulation tool with its own assumptions.

maths.step: How precise each point on the chart is
maths.text: Each point is the mean idle time over 30 instances, with a 95% confidence interval. For the Briskorn rule at 12 AGVs the standard deviation over the instances is $s$ below.

cards.title: With twelve AGVs every rule needs to see ten jobs ahead
cards.lead: Ten jobs. With 1, 2 or 3 jobs in view, every rule leaves the cranes waiting at least 24 s per container at 12 AGVs, because loads are fetched too late. With 5 jobs the three real rules reach 5.6 to 6.7 s, and with 10 jobs 3.4 to 3.9 s. All three real rules do best at 10 on the training instances, and seeing further adds nothing.
cards.body: NV/FCFS reaches 3.4 s with 10 jobs against 6.3 s with 5, so it now uses the same window as the terminal, which shows every method the next 10 jobs, as in Kim and Bae (2004). Random dispatching is the exception. It does better with 5 jobs, 6.2 s against 7.8 s, because a short window caps how many AGVs one crane can collect, so the window itself does part of the dispatching. The terminal keeps 10 jobs, since the look-ahead is a property of the terminal and not a setting to tune, and the random reference is always measured with it.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. AGVs drive at up to 6 m/s when empty and 3.5 m/s when carrying a container (Zhao et al., 2025), turn on a 10 m radius (Luo, 2016b) and share the roads: each AGV books the road ahead of it, its body plus its braking distance, so AGVs wait for each other and never collide (model v5). No randomness.
1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50 jobs per crane. The terminal and the rule use the same window here.
The terminal shows 10 jobs to every method (Kim and Bae, 2004), and NV/FCFS uses the same window of 10 (D-41).

With 10 AGVs every rule is best at 5 jobs, since a window of 5 caps each crane at five AGVs, the fair share of ten. With 14 AGVs the real rules are best at 10 jobs or more, NV/FCFS 3.1 s against 14.8 s at 5.
The Briskorn inventory rule with phase factor 1.6 (Briskorn et al., 2006), nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS) with a window of 10 jobs, fixed crane groups, and random dispatching.
30 seeds, with every method run on the same seeds. Means are shown with a 95% confidence interval (t = 2.045).
cards.label: Experiment 2.2 · Look-ahead window

design.question: How many upcoming jobs of each crane must a rule see to dispatch well on this yard?
design.why: A rule sees only the next few jobs of each crane, called the look-ahead window. A load has to be fetched from the yard before the crane needs it, so a rule that sees too few jobs sends its AGVs too late.
design.vary: The window, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 50 jobs per crane, for all four rules, at 12 AGVs and at 10 and 14 as side cases.
design.fixed: No randomness, with the same yard and instances as the fleet sweep. The window is chosen on 30 training instances and reported on the 30 test instances used everywhere else, so no rule is tuned on the numbers it is judged by.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container on the test instances, with a 95% confidence interval.
design.decide: For each rule, the window with the lowest idle time on the training instances, and the shorter window when two are equal to one decimal.

maths.step: When a rule first sees a job
maths.text: A job becomes visible when the job $w$ places ahead of it in the crane\'s sequence is handed over. With a crane cycle of $c = 75$ s, a job is therefore seen about $w$ cycles before the crane needs it.

maths.step: Why three jobs are too few on this yard
maths.text: To fetch a load, an AGV must drive to the block, visit the rack and come back, which takes about the AGV work per container $\bar W$ found in the fleet sweep. The lead time must cover it. The scene below grows the window one job at a time, and it can be paused or stepped through.

maths.step: Choosing a window without favouring any rule
maths.text: Each rule\'s window is chosen on 30 training instances (seeds 100 to 129) and the result is reported on the 30 test instances (seeds 0 to 29) used by every other experiment. Ties at one decimal go to the shorter window.

cards.title: The size of the ship does not change the comparison
cards.lead: It does not. From 100 to 400 jobs per crane the three real rules stay within 0.6 s of their standard result, and random dispatching stays far behind. Bigger bays do lower the waiting, to 1.7 s for NV/FCFS, because the crane switches from discharge to loading less often.
cards.body: The three real rules are always within a second of each other at 12 AGVs, and random dispatching wastes about 5 s more per container at every size. The smallest ship, 24 jobs per crane, is distorted by the start of the run and is not used. With crane times varying by 20%, and with 10 and 14 AGVs, the picture is the same. The full table is in the method details. This completes stage 2, so every later experiment uses 12 AGVs, a look-ahead of 10 jobs for every method, and the standard ship.

cards.label: Experiment 2.3 · Size of the ship

design.question: Would a longer or shorter ship change how the methods compare?
design.why: Every experiment uses one standard ship of 100 jobs per crane. If a different ship ranked the methods differently, the results would hold for this ship only.
design.vary: The ship, from 1 bay of 12 discharge and 12 load containers per crane up to 8 bays of 25 and 25, and 2 bigger bays of 50 and 50. All four rules, with crane times fixed and varying by up to 20%.
design.fixed: 12 AGVs, with 10 and 14 as side cases, the 50-block yard, and the same 30 instances for every rule.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container and the order of the rules, with 95% confidence intervals.
design.decide: The standard ship is large enough if the idle time per container and the order of the rules stay the same from it upward.

bars.note: Jobs per crane, bays × (discharge + load). Bars are means over 30 instances with 95% intervals. Hover over a group to read the values.

tableTop.caption: Crane idle per container in seconds, 12 AGVs, no randomness, 30 instances. Bays are worked in order, each bay its discharge containers first and then its load containers.

maths.step: Bay changes per container
maths.text: Each crane works its bays in order, first the $n_d$ discharge containers of a bay and then its $n_l$ load containers. At the switch to loading the crane needs a container that has to be fetched from far away, so it often waits there. The number of bay changes per container is $\sigma$.

maths.step: A two-number model of the waiting
maths.text: Suppose each container costs a base waiting $a$, and each bay change adds $s$ seconds. The two ships with 200 jobs per crane differ only in their bay size, so fixed groups at the operating fleet give both numbers.

maths.step: Checking the model on the other ships
maths.text: With 4 or 8 bays of 25 and 25 the number of bay changes per container is the same as on the standard ship, so the model predicts the same waiting, and that is what the simulator gives. Only the smallest ship, 24 jobs per crane, lies below the model, because its run is too short for the waiting to settle.

maths.step: Four times as many containers, same answer
maths.text: The gap between the largest ship and the standard one is measured instance by instance, for the Briskorn rule at the operating fleet. It is small, so the standard ship of 100 jobs per crane is large enough.

cards.title: The search comes close to the best dispatching at the operating fleet
cards.lead: At 12 AGVs the search recovers 90 to 100% of the room for improvement and finds the exact best in most instances. With only 6 AGVs, where the best plans are harder to find, it recovers 81 to 99%.
cards.body: The weakest case at the operating fleet is the medium ship with crane times fixed, where the search ends 0.19 s per container above the exact best on average. So the benchmark is close to the true best but not always equal to it, and any gap between a rule and the benchmark understates the true gap a little. On these tiny ships random dispatching is sometimes close to the rules, because a run of 6 or 8 jobs per crane is dominated by its start, as Experiment 2.3 showed. That is why the rules themselves are compared on the standard ship.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. AGVs drive at up to 6 m/s when empty and 3.5 m/s when carrying a container (Zhao et al., 2025), turn on a 10 m radius (Luo, 2016b) and share the roads: each AGV books the road ahead of it, its body plus its braking distance, so AGVs wait for each other and never collide (model v5).
2 cranes with 3 discharge and 3 load containers each (924 order lists, 20 instances), and with 4 and 4 (12,870 order lists, 10 instances).

Memetic search on order lists (a genetic algorithm combined with local search), started from the rules' own orders. Budgets of 150 and 300 simulator runs on the small ship and 1,000 on the medium one, which is 8% of all its order lists. Best of 3 runs with seeds 0, 1 and 2.

design.question: How close does our search come to the best possible dispatching, on ships small enough to know the best exactly?
design.why: Later experiments compare each rule with a perfect-information benchmark, a dispatcher that knows every crane time in advance. That benchmark comes from a search, the memetic algorithm, and not from an exact solver, so it may miss the true best. Before it is used, we measure how much it misses.
design.vary: Two small ships, 12 and 16 jobs, on 20 and 10 instances. Fleets of 12 AGVs (operating) and 6 (scarce). Crane times fixed and varying by ±30%.
design.fixed: The current yard and rules. On these ships every one of the 924 or 12,870 order lists is simulated, which gives the exact best. The search runs three times per case with fixed seeds.
design.measure: How far the search ends above the exact best, how often it finds it, and the share of the rules' room for improvement it recovers.
design.decide: The search is fit to serve as the benchmark if it recovers nearly all of the room at the operating fleet. Wherever it misses, the benchmark is read as "at least this much better than the rules".

maths.step: Why the best cannot simply be computed for a real ship
maths.text: A dispatching plan here is an order list. It says, for each of the $m$ jobs in turn, which crane the next free AGV serves. Half the jobs belong to each crane, so the number of different order lists is a binomial coefficient.

maths.step: Room for improvement, and how much of it the search finds
maths.text: For each instance, $\bar I^{*}$ is the exact best over all order lists, $\bar I_{\text{rule}}$ the best of the three rules and $\bar I_{\text{search}}$ the best of three search runs. The room is the distance from the rule to the best, and $\rho$ is the share of it the search recovers. The example below uses the averages of one case. The table averages $\rho$ instance by instance, which gives a slightly different figure.

maths.step: Reading the benchmark later
maths.text: The search can miss the best but never beat it, so the idle time of the benchmark is never below the true best. A rule that is $\Delta$ seconds above the benchmark is therefore at least $\Delta$ seconds above the true best.
maths.tex: $$\bar I^{*} \le \bar I_{\text{search}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar I_{\text{rule}} - \bar I^{*} \ge \bar I_{\text{rule}} - \bar I_{\text{search}}$$

cards.title: A plan made in advance loses its lead once crane times vary, and much room remains
cards.lead: With fixed crane times the plan made in advance beats the best rule (NV/FCFS) clearly, 1.1 s of idle per container against 3.4 s, ahead on all 30 instances. At ±40% its lead is gone, −0.02 ± 0.65 s, and it is ahead on only 16 of the 30 instances. A dispatcher that knew every crane time in advance would still need only 1.4 s, so about 1.8 s per container, 57% of the rules' waiting, is left to win.
cards.body: The rules suffer only mildly, since they react to what actually happens. NV/FCFS rises from 3.4 to 4.1 s, fixed groups from 3.9 to 4.3 s, and the Briskorn rule to 4.2 s. A plan whose AGVs keep their planned routes is worse than every real rule as soon as the crane times vary by 10%, reaching 5.9 s at ±40%. Keeping only the planned order of jobs, and letting any free AGV take the next one, holds up better. The benchmark stays between 1.1 and 1.4 s at every level. Random dispatching is far behind and is hidden in the chart. So a plan made in advance fades under randomness, and the rules leave a large gap. Closing that gap in real time is the job of the learning dispatcher.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. AGVs drive at up to 6 m/s when empty and 3.5 m/s when carrying a container (Zhao et al., 2025), turn on a 10 m radius (Luo, 2016b) and share the roads: each AGV books the road ahead of it, its body plus its braking distance, so AGVs wait for each other and never collide (model v5). 12 AGVs.
Each crane cycle is drawn uniformly between 75(1 − δ) and 75(1 + δ) s, once per container, with the same draws for every method. δ takes the values 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4.
The Briskorn inventory rule with phase factor 1.6 (Briskorn et al., 2006), nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS) with a window of 10 jobs, fixed crane groups, and random dispatching.

One memetic search per instance on the planned crane times, 10,000 simulator runs, seed 0. Carried out in two ways. With the job order kept, the planned order in which jobs get an AGV is fixed and whichever AGV is free takes the next job. With the AGV routes kept, each AGV follows its own planned list of cranes.

Best of 3 memetic searches, seeds 0, 1 and 2, with 10,000 simulator runs each, told the realised crane times in advance. The 3 runs differ by 0.27 s per container on average at ±40%, and 328 of the 390 searches were still improving in the last 30% of their budget. So the benchmark is the best plan known, not a proven best, and the room for improvement is a lower bound. Experiment 3.1 found that the search recovers 90 to 100% of the room at 12 AGVs on small ships.
The 390 searches took 154 minutes on 56 cores (server log in results_reference). Every search is saved, so the table is regenerated from them in about a minute on any computer.
30 seeds, with every method run on the same seeds. Means are shown with a 95% confidence interval (t = 2.045). Leads and gaps are measured instance by instance.

design.question: How do the rules, a plan made in advance and a dispatcher that knows the future cope when crane times vary?
design.why: Real crane cycles are not exactly 75 s. Studies that optimise a schedule beforehand, with a GA or a MIP, assume they are. This experiment shows what that assumption costs, and how much better a dispatcher could still do.
design.vary: How much each crane cycle varies, from fixed (±0%) to ±40%. The methods are the four rules, a plan made once on the planned crane times and carried out in two ways, and the perfect-information benchmark.
design.fixed: 12 AGVs, the standard ship of 100 jobs per crane, a look-ahead of 10 jobs, and the same 30 instances and crane-time draws for every method.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container with 95% confidence intervals, the lead of the plan over the best rule, and the gap of each method to the benchmark.
design.decide: A method copes with randomness if its idle time stays low as δ grows. The gap to the benchmark shows how much a better real-time dispatcher could still gain.

maths.step: How the crane times vary
maths.text: Each crane cycle is drawn once per container, uniformly around the planned $\bar c = 75$ s, as in *Kim and Bae (2004)*. The draw is fixed by the seed, so every method meets exactly the same crane times.

maths.step: The lead of a plan made in advance
maths.text: The plan is optimised once on the planned crane times, then followed while the real times vary. Its lead $L$ is how much less the cranes wait than with NV/FCFS, the strongest rule here, measured instance by instance.

maths.step: Room left for a better dispatcher
maths.text: For each instance, $I_{\text{rule}}$ is the best of the three real rules and $I_{\text{PI}}$ the perfect-information benchmark. Their average gap $R$ is the room for improvement, and $R / \bar I_{\text{rule}}$ is the share of the rules\' waiting that a perfect dispatcher would remove.

maths.step: Reading the benchmark
maths.text: The benchmark is the best of 3 search runs, and the search can miss the true best but never beat it. So a rule that is $R$ seconds above the benchmark is at least $R$ seconds above the true best. At ±0% only one run was made, since the plan made once is the same problem. Compared one run against one run, the benchmark rises gently with $\delta$.

cards.title: Re-planning makes the GA the strongest traditional method, but it cannot see the future
cards.lead: Re-planning works. It beats the plan made once at every level of randomness, by 1.1 ± 0.5 s per container at ±40%. Its lead over the best rule on each instance shrinks as randomness grows, from 1.04 ± 0.26 s at ±10% to 0.23 ± 0.33 s at ±40%, which is no longer clear. And its gap to the benchmark grows from 0.7 s to 1.6 s, because it plans with crane times it cannot know.
cards.body: So the GA with re-planning is the strongest traditional method, and the one a learning dispatcher has to beat. Its weakness shows in its own numbers. At ±40% its re-plans together expected to save 11.6 s per container, yet only 1.1 s survived the real crane times. With fixed crane times it even ends below the benchmark, 1.03 s against 1.13 s, since re-planning is then just more search on the same problem. This confirms that the benchmark is the best plan known, not a proven best. A re-plan took 43 to 57 s on average, within one crane cycle. Experiment 4.3 asks what happens when the terminal has to wait for it.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. AGVs drive at up to 6 m/s when empty and 3.5 m/s when carrying a container (Zhao et al., 2025), turn on a 10 m radius (Luo, 2016b) and share the roads: each AGV books the road ahead of it, its body plus its braking distance, so AGVs wait for each other and never collide (model v5). 12 AGVs.
As in Experiment 4.1, the same draws.

Starts from the plan made once in Experiment 4.1 (10,000 simulator runs, before the ship arrives). After every 10 crane handovers the rest of the order list is re-optimised by a memetic search of 500 simulator runs, started from the remaining old plan and from the three rules continued from the present. The decisions already taken are kept, and replaying them reproduces the present exactly, since the simulator is deterministic. Re-planning when events happen follows *Günther, Grunow and Lehmann (2005)*.
Real crane times of the containers handed over so far, the planned 75 s for the rest. The future draws are never used.
Two automatic tests: the replay reproduces the present state exactly, and with fixed crane times re-planning never makes the plan worse.

design.question: If the GA re-plans while the ship is worked, does it keep its lead when crane times vary?
design.why: Experiment 4.1 showed that a plan made in advance loses most of its lead under randomness. The obvious answer is to re-plan as the terminal evolves, as dispatching systems do in practice. Only if re-planning also falls short is a learning dispatcher needed.
design.vary: How much crane cycles vary, from ±0% to ±40%. The GA starts from the plan of Experiment 4.1 and re-plans after every 10 crane handovers, keeping the decisions already taken.
design.fixed: 12 AGVs, the standard ship, and the same 30 instances and crane-time draws as Experiment 4.1, so every method is compared instance by instance. Each re-plan is a memetic search of 500 simulator runs.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container, the gain over the plan made once and over the best rule, the gap to the benchmark, and the computing time of one re-plan.
design.decide: Re-planning is the stronger traditional method if it beats both the plan made once and the rules. What is left between it and the benchmark is what a dispatcher that anticipates better could still win.

maths.step: When the GA re-plans
maths.text: The plan is re-made after every $k = 10$ crane handovers. A ship of $n = 200$ containers gives at most the number below. The last re-plans are skipped when fewer than three jobs are left to re-order, so each ship here gets 18.

maths.step: What the GA knows at a re-plan
maths.text: At time $t$ the GA uses the real crane time $c_i$ of every container already handed over, and of a crane\'s current container if the crane is already waiting for it. For every other container it assumes the planned $\bar c = 75$ s, or the time already elapsed if that is longer. This is the same information the rules have.
maths.tex: $$\tilde c_i(t) = \begin{cases} c_i & \text{container } i \text{ handed over, or its crane ready, by } t\\[2pt] \max(\bar c,\ t - h_{i-1}) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

maths.step: What re-planning thinks it gains, and what it gains
maths.text: Each re-plan compares the old plan with the new one under its own assumptions. Adding these believed gains over all re-plans and comparing with the real gain over the plan made once shows how much of each improvement survives the crane times that actually happen. With fixed crane times the two must agree, and they do.

maths.step: Fast enough for real time
maths.text: A re-plan must finish before it is needed. One re-plan of 500 simulator runs took on average the time below on one core of the server, with 56 searches sharing the machine, less than one crane cycle. That is about 0.1 s per simulator run, the speed Experiment 4.3 uses to charge the thinking time.

cards.title: Once its thinking time counts, re-planning is no better than the best rule
cards.lead: At ±40%, with 1.6 to 183.6 s per re-plan, the GA waits 3.40 to 3.50 s per container. That is 0.6 to 0.7 s less than the plan it starts from, but no better than the best rule on each instance, +0.20 to +0.30 s. Every version stays more than 2 s above the benchmark.
cards.body: Waiting 54 s for each plan costs 0.43 ± 0.26 s per container at ±40% against the same search made instantly. A faster search does not help either, since it finds worse plans. At ±20% re-planning still pays. 54 s per re-plan gives 2.29 s, 0.64 ± 0.22 s below the best rule, while 183.6 s makes it worse again, 2.60 s, because the plan arrives late and is built on times that have already changed. The best rule here is picked per instance after the fact. Against the single best rule, NV/FCFS, re-planning with 54 s per re-plan stays 0.65 ± 0.41 s better at ±40%. With fixed crane times the 54 s search ends at 1.05 s, just below the benchmark of Experiment 4.1, which again shows that the benchmark is a best-known plan. So no traditional method closes the gap in real time.

design.question: If every re-plan takes real time, during which the AGVs keep following the old plan, is re-planning still worth it?

maths.step: Thinking time of one re-plan
maths.text: A re-plan simulates $n$ candidate plans, and one simulator run took about $\tau_1 = 0.108$ s on the server in Experiment 4.2. The thinking time grows with the size of the search.

maths.step: What the AGVs do while the GA thinks
maths.text: The re-plan $r$ starts at time $t_r$ and plans on the state at that moment. Its plan is used only from $t_r + \tau$. Until then the AGVs keep following the previous plan, so decisions taken meanwhile are the old plan\'s.
maths.tex: $$\text{decision at } t \text{ follows } \begin{cases} \pi_{r-1} & t_r \le t < t_r + \tau\\[2pt] \pi_r & t \ge t_r + \tau \end{cases}$$

maths.step: The price of thinking
maths.text: The same search of 500 runs is compared with and without its thinking time, instance by instance. The difference $C$ is what waiting for the plan costs.

maths.step: What fast re-planning adds to the plan made in advance
maths.text: The gain $\Delta$ of the re-planning GA over the plan it starts from, instance by instance. A value near zero means the fast re-plans change little.
